title: Playing piano rags on clarinet and the Polites-Coyle Ragtimers
summary: Brass fatigue led him to feature rags like Perfect Rag, learned from records, improvised on, and played at conventions with pianist Graham Coyle.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: What we played: tunes and repertoire in the early days

blocks.x: Oh yeah, yeah, and he would discuss how Mutt would change his whole phrasing and tone from one chorus to another. Yes, yes. And change the whole sound of the band. Yes, yes, yes. What about your own repertoire of tunes that you feature on clarinet?

Ah yes, well of course I don't like feature melodies and things, but we found out very very soon, very quickly when we went to England, we were playing sessions every night, that the brass men just couldn't keep up with it, lips would be shattered and so on, so that I'd have to do some numbers occasionally and it wasn't too bad because it gave me an opportunity to feature things that I used to play around with at home a bit. I like getting onto rags and piano rags and playing them on clarinet and trying to play them fairly authentically, get all the sort of phrases and things in as much as a single melody line can do it. But, and then to use them as a vehicle for improvising in the last few choruses. So I was doing quite a bit of that sort of stuff in the last couple of years and I've had great fun playing things like Perfect Rag, Nonsense Rag, quite a few of the Tony Parenti ones. In fact one that he wrote, Crawfish Crawl, things like that. It's, I've had quite fun playing those. They're different again. I play less like Lewis then. Somewhere I'll find a style that's mine eventually I suppose.
What's strange do you use when you, you hear me, improvise?
I don't, I don't have any set rule. I just try to find the, the part that seems to sit first. I suppose it's generally the trio because it generally sits first, but not all those.
Perfect Rag I know that I go back to the first part. Although, the fact is that I do improvise on the trio a little bit before I go back to the first part.
And you modulate back to the original key.
Yes, yes, modulate back to the original one. Instead of doing that.
Now, you can, do you listen to the record of Perfect Rag or do you look at the sheet music of it or?
No, I do it off the record. I always have. From the record.

I got it from the old Jolly 1923 Genet I think, recording of Perfect Drag. I think that was it. I just played it over and over and over and over again until I got a melody out of it and got some idea of the chords. What I have done each year at the jazz conventions for quite a few years, I've teamed up with a very fine pianist, probably our best pianist in Australia, Graham Coyle. We've played, we had what we call the Polites Coyle Ragtimers, just as a name of a group, playing only at the jazz convention. And it's become a bit of an institution at the jazz conventions. We play all these rag-type tunes.
